claim: Believable conclusions are accepted far more often than unbelievable ones, and the pull is strongest on invalid arguments (accepting believable-invalid is the dominant error). Aggregate 80% vs 33% accepted; Stupple and Ball N=48 invalid 71/36 and 61/25.
agent_test: Same argument set with believable, unbelievable and nonsense-word contents; measure the valid rate on invalid-believable items at equal tokens with and without the check step.

claim: The classic logic-by-belief interaction (belief effect larger on invalid than valid) is replicated in raw endorsement rates, but whether it reflects reasoning quality is contested: ROC/SDT work says it is a response-bias artefact. Gap search: the classic acceptance rates exist in two versions in secondary text (92/46/92/8 in Trippas 2018, Macchi 2019 and a popular summary; 89/56/71/10 in Wikipedia and one article); primary paper now read: Exp 1 92/46/92/8 (N=24), Exp 2 86/62/66/13 (N=64), Exp 3 91/53/67/6 (N=32); interaction p<.01 in Exp 2, p=.067 in Exp 3.
schema_part: none (measurement rule: do not score our agent with the interaction index)
agent_test: Score agent runs with d-prime from confidence ratings, not raw difference scores; compare conclusions from both.

claim: Hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of 22 ROC studies (N=993) finds no average difference in discrimination (da) between believable and unbelievable syllogisms (BF 7.34 for null); ROCs fit equal-variance SDT (BF 17.28 and 11.84). Belief acts mostly as response bias. Authors are SDT proponents.
schema_part: G (guard targets bias in the answer threshold, not the reasoning)
agent_test: Check whether a content-blind re-asking of the verdict changes the criterion (bias) or the ability (d-prime) of the agent.

claim: Dissent on the ROC reading: Klauer and Kellen (2011) argue ROCs for binary responses are linear and the curvilinear result comes from aggregation; Singmann and Kellen (2014) show the 2x2 SDT design is unidentifiable. Not fully resolved by the 2018 meta-analysis (shared authors with the SDT camp).
agent_test: None direct; treat as a caution on interpreting any single index.

claim: Belief effects on discrimination are moderated: believability hurt accuracy only on complex syllogisms (Trippas 2013) and only in higher-ability reasoners (Trippas 2014, N=76). The pooled null hides moderators.
agent_test: Split items by difficulty; compare belief-driven errors at equal tokens, easy vs hard.

claim: Time pressure raises belief bias and lowers logical accuracy (Evans and Curtis-Holmes 2005, 10 s limit), mostly on conflict items. A parallel-processing study (Trippas, Thompson, Handley 2017, N=45 and N=84) did not support a simple fast-belief-then-slow-logic sequence: conflict items were harder (.68 vs .83) but belief judgments were not clearly faster. Gap search: no direct failed replication of the 10 s deadline was found, but Trippas, Thompson and Handley 2017 and a 2015 thesis favour a parallel-processing reading; not settled. Further boundary conditions: speeded conditional inference left belief bias unchanged (Evans, Handley, Bacon 2009), and under time pressure the accuracy cost of believability vanished in an ROC analysis (Trippas, Handley, Verde 2013, abstract level).
agent_test: Run the agent with a short vs long reasoning budget on conflict items; measure the belief-consistent error rate.

claim: Conflict (belief and logic disagree) is harder and slower than no-conflict: inspection times longer on conflict problems, accuracy lower.
schema_part: S (conflict-detection state) / O (verify when verdict and prior belief disagree)
agent_test: Tag items by whether the model's prior belief about the conclusion matches its derived verdict; allocate extra verification only on mismatch vs uniformly, at equal tokens.

claim: Instruction wording matters: 'must be true' alone did not remove belief bias (Evans 1994), but asking 'does the conclusion NECESSARILY follow?' raised correct rejection of an invalid-believable item from 4% (plain wording) to 66% (untrained) and 77% (trained); 'criteria of logic' wording gave 41% and 67%. Macchi 2019 used ONE item per condition. Gap search: Newstead 1992 Exp 5 long instructions gave 83% correct rejection of invalid-believable items but Evans 1994 got 56% with the same instructions; Macchi's 66% to 77% 'necessarily' result is one item per condition and earlier multi-item necessity wordings are reported unsuccessful. Original data (d21, d23): the Exp 1 instruction already said 'necessarily follow' yet 92% accepted invalid-believable items; the stronger Exp 3 wording gave 67%. Different designs, so only suggestive.
agent_test: A/B the prompt wording ('follow' vs 'necessarily follow') on a battery of many invalid-believable items, not one.

claim: Misinterpreted necessity: belief bias is concentrated in indeterminate invalid syllogisms (conclusion possible but not forced); on determinately invalid items the interaction disappears (Newstead 1992 Exps 1-2). Gap search: Newstead 1992 Exp 1-2 report the interaction vanishing with only determinate syllogisms (abstract-level evidence only). The 1983 paper itself named both misinterpreted necessity and selective scrutiny as candidate explanations and could not separate them (d24).
schema_part: O (search for a counter-model before accepting)
agent_test: Compare agent acceptance of 'possible but not necessary' vs 'determinately false' believable conclusions; add a 'find a counterexample' step and see which class improves.

claim: Selective scrutiny (scrutinise only unbelievable conclusions) has mixed support: eye-tracking and inspection-time data (Ball 2006, Stupple and Ball 2008) fit selective processing or parallel conflict models better than classic scrutiny or mental models; Thompson 2003 found more time on believable conclusions.
schema_part: O (uniform scrutiny: verify believable conclusions too)
agent_test: Compare verifying only conclusions the model dislikes vs verifying all, at equal tokens.

claim: Individual differences: higher cognitive ability and analytic thinking disposition go with better accuracy and lower belief response bias; religious skeptics made fewer conflict errors; statistical-strategy reasoners are more swayed than counterexample reasoners; older adults more biased.
agent_test: Prompt a counterexample strategy vs a likelihood ('seems plausible') strategy; compare belief bias rates.

claim: Disfluent presentation did not reduce belief bias and lowered accuracy (da .92 fluent vs .51 disfluent, N=76).
agent_test: Low priority; no clear LLM analogue.

claim: LLMs show the human pattern: 'valid' for believable conclusions, high sensitivity but low specificity, item-level accuracy correlated with humans (t(345)=4.98). Effects persist without instructions, with few-shot examples and with instruction tuning. Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5 (older models).
schema_part: G (guard needed for the model itself)
agent_test: Replicate on our model with believable/unbelievable/nonsense contents; report the valid-rate gap.

claim: Content effects are not fixed by scale or prompting alone in older open models (Bertolazzi 2024: LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot CoT 30.31% on the believable set, 0.83% on invalid items; atmosphere heuristic predicts 82.97% of invalid-schema errors); fine-tuning raises accuracy to 96.25% (not shown to remove bias; table columns garbled). Gap search: in 2025-26 data, GPT-4o-class and older chat models still show large gaps while recent reasoning models are near ceiling (see K19, K21).
agent_test: Run chain-of-thought vs plain on our model with equal tokens on the content-effect set.

claim: Newer instruction-tuned models with CoT cut content effects a lot (Qwen2.5-32B CE 0.348 to 0.096; Qwen3-14B 0.213 to 0.014), and activation steering cuts them more; this partly conflicts with K14 and shows the picture depends on model generation. Gap search: for FregeLogic's open models CoT did not uniformly cut the content effect (Maverick few-shot CoT CE 3.83 to 10.11); for GPT-4o a CoT prompt rescued 87% of earlier failures (selected failures, no matched control). Frontier CoT at equal tokens is still untested.
agent_test: Measure CE for our model with plain vs CoT prompting; steering is outside a prompt-only scaffold.

claim: Formalise-then-prove: translating to first-order logic and having a prover decide validity removes most content effect (LINC beats CoT by 10-38 points on ProofWriter; SemEval-2026 UFAL-CUNI 95.29% / 97.37% accuracy). The official CE metric is noisy at high accuracy. Gap search correction: this holds for weak or mid models (Qwen3 4B: 95.83% / CE 2.28 with Prover9 vs 84.17% / CE 14.67 end-to-end) but not for a strong model on easy syllogisms (gemini-3-flash LLM-only 98.43% / bias 2.13 vs 100 / 0.0). A solver on LLM-extracted structure alone was worse than prompting (Z3 only 74.7%, CE 26.28). Solver pipelines cost 4x to 15x CoT (CLOVER $0.30 vs $0.02) and about 4,300 tokens per item in FregeLogic. No equal-token comparison exists.
schema_part: O (formalise and check with a tool)
agent_test: Syllogism subset: LLM-to-logic plus a checker vs CoT at equal tokens; measure CE.

claim: Abstracting content away (replace nouns with variables or quasi-symbols) before reasoning is a plausible prompt-level remedy; nonsense-word items still show some 'valid' lean. Gap search: predicate-argument abstraction scored worse than raw text (77.48% vs 92.10%) while staying near canonical syllogism notation scored best (98.95%), so abstraction is not automatically helpful; no equal-token test.
agent_test: Run the same item with real and symbolised terms and compare verdict agreement; adopt the symbolic verdict when they disagree.

claim: Belief bias scales with belief strength (prototypical > nonprototypical > nonword, N=102: 2.65, 2.25, 1.43 of 5 accepted) and priming the category changes it. Gap search: no LLM study of graded belief strength was found; the LLM papers treat plausibility as binary.
agent_test: Grade conclusion plausibility and check the dose-response of error on it in our agent.

claim: Recent strong models show little belief bias on easy categorical syllogisms: in 14 models Gemini 2.5 Pro / Flash, GPT-OSS-20B and GLM-4.6 differ by 0.8 to 1.9 pp between congruent and incongruent items, Kimi-K2 and DeepSeek V3.1 by about 7.5 to 7.9 pp, while smaller models reach +28 to +47 pp (mean +10.81, d=0.66, 12 of 14 positive). These are accuracy differences at ceiling, not d-prime.
agent_test: Score our model with d-prime and criterion per cell on hard (multiple-model) syllogisms, not only easy ones.

claim: A strong 2023 model (GPT-4) shows the human pattern in SDT terms on the BaRDa entailments: d' about 1.21 for believable (true-fact) items vs 1.96 for unbelievable, criterion c -0.81 vs +0.30 (my calculation from the paper's cell accuracies). GPT-3.5: d' 0.81 vs 1.22, c -0.90 vs +0.41. Both sensitivity and criterion move.
agent_test: Report hit rate, false-alarm rate, d' and c per believability cell for our agent.

claim: Reasoning effort, not scale, drives performance on valid-but-unbelievable items: GPT-5-nano went from 69.2% (minimum effort) to 98.8% (medium), GPT-5-mini 99.7%, while GPT-4o scored 79.5% and the deprecated Claude-3-sonnet / Claude-3-opus scored 20.3% / 7.2%. Items are all valid, so over-rejection (a criterion shift) cannot be told apart from poor logic.
agent_test: Include invalid items; vary reasoning budget on the same items and compare d' and c.

claim: Gap 3 is not closed: the 'necessarily follows' wording effect (66% to 77% correct rejection vs 4% to 10% control) rests on one syllogism per condition, earlier multi-item necessity wordings are reported unsuccessful, and long instructions replicated only partly (83% in Newstead 1992 Exp 5 vs 56% in Evans 1994). No LLM transfer test was found.
agent_test: Run 3 or more wordings (plain, 'necessarily', 'could it be false') over 40+ items with indeterminate and determinate invalid cases.

claim: Routing extra verification only to uncertain items helps a little: calling Z3 only on 3-2 ensemble splits (7.9% of items) raised accuracy 93.4 to 94.3 and cut content effect 3.39 to 2.85, with 19 correct and 11 wrong flips; widening Z3's authority or vetoing high-consensus answers hurt (91.7%, 74.1%). The trigger was disagreement among models, not a belief-conflict flag.
agent_test: Compare: verify only when model prior belief about the conclusion disagrees with its derived verdict vs verify all vs verify random subset at equal tokens.

claim: Prover-on-extracted-structure carries an invalid-lean error: Z3 alone was 98% right on invalid items but about 52% on valid items because extraction mistakes break valid chains; 11 of 11 wrong flips rejected valid syllogisms, 8 with unbelievable content.
agent_test: Treat a prover 'invalid' verdict on a model-believed-valid item as a prompt to re-extract, not as a final answer.

claim: Cost of the stronger-checker designs is high and unmatched: FregeLogic about 4,300 tokens and 6 calls per item; CLOVER $0.30 vs CoT $0.02 on AR-LSAT. No source compares prover, abstraction, selective verification and plain CoT at equal tokens.
agent_test: Equal-token comparison: self-consistency vote vs normalise-then-parse vs selective verification.

claim: RESOLVED from the primary paper (Evans, Barston, Pollard 1983, read in full). Exp 1 (N=24): valid-believable 92, valid-unbelievable 46, invalid-believable 92, invalid-unbelievable 8. Exp 2 (N=64): 86/62/66/13. Exp 3 (N=32): 91/53/67/6. Wikipedia's 89/56/71/10 matches no cell exactly (nearest is Exp 2 A-C conclusions, 88/56/72/13). Correct when logic agrees with belief vs conflicts: 92 vs 27 (Exp 1), 87 vs 48 (Exp 2), 97 vs 43 (Exp 3).
agent_test: Cite invalid-believable acceptance as 66-92% across the three original experiments.

claim: No source was found, for humans or LLMs, that tests: counterexample search split by determinate versus indeterminate invalid items; verification of only unbelievable conclusions vs all at equal tokens; a belief-versus-verdict conflict flag as an error predictor in LLMs; or LLM error against graded belief strength. These tests need to be run, not read.
agent_test: Run the four experiments on our model.

claim: Both later theories come from the 1983 discussion. People who accepted valid-unbelievable conclusions cited premises more (X2=24.61) and irrelevant facts less (X2=15.11) than those who rejected them. The data do not separate selective scrutiny from misinterpreted necessity.
agent_test: Run gaps 4 and 5 as experiments: counterexample step split by determinate and indeterminate invalid items, and verify-only-conflict vs verify-all at equal tokens.

claim: Answer format and item type decide whether a strong model's content effect shows. GPT-4 (2023) had no drop on incongruent items in multiple choice with no 'none follows' option (90.00 vs 80.00 English; 97.5 vs 100 Japanese) but fell from 82.92 to 67.23 on incongruent NLI items. A predicate-logic translation written in the same prompt lifted GPT-4 from 77.78 to 96.67 on a 90-item set.
schema_part: G (answer format must allow 'does not follow') / O (formalise inside the prompt)
agent_test: Always include a 'does not follow' option; compare plain vs translate-then-judge at equal tokens on indeterminate items.

claim: The effect of time pressure on belief bias is task- and measure-specific: no change in speeded conditional inference (2009), and the accuracy cost of believability vanished under time pressure in an ROC analysis (2013, abstract level). With Trippas 2017 this means 'rushed means more belief bias' is not safe to carry to the agent.
agent_test: Vary reasoning budget and score d-prime and criterion separately.

claim: After extra searching, no d-prime or criterion analysis of current Claude, GPT-5 or o-series models on belief-bias syllogisms, and no token-matched comparison of chain-of-thought, prover, selective verification or conflict-flag routing, was found. Gaps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 10 remain experiments to run.
agent_test: Build the hard-item set (indeterminate invalid, believable and unbelievable, graded plausibility) and run it on the target model at matched token budgets.
